exact_source_sections.text: The most significant change that Reaper difficulty brings is the chance to encounter Reapers themselves.

Each time an enemy spawns there's a chance a Reaper spawns too, and this chance is higher the more Skulls you select. They spawn at the last location of the associated enemy (even if inaccessible) and there's a ~5 second delay before they appear. Reapers have their own logic and will not follow special scripted enemy pathing. (Since Update 81, monsters spawned by other monsters, such as Oozes that split from larger Oozes and Mephits summoned by other Mephits, cannot trigger a Reaper to spawn when they spawn or are slain.)

paragraphs: Introduced in Update 24 and reworked in Update 34, some enemies gain randomized buffs on Hard, Elite, and Reaper difficulties in quests with an effective level of 5 or higher (i.e. starting with level 4 quests on Hard difficulty, and level 3 quests on Elite or Reaper). These enemies are called Champions, and they have an always-visible, unless sneaking or invisible, burning crown above their heads to mark them.

Monster Champions do not spawn in any quest on Solo, Casual, or Normal difficulty; nearly all raids (except Killing Time and Legendary Shroud's Part 5, where enemies are granted champion buffs but cannot drop Remnants); nor any wilderness area (with the singular exception of Balthan Korl, who again cannot drop Remnants). Furthermore, Reapers and red-named and purple-named enemies cannot spawn as Champions.

Not all champions are alike: some are tougher (Tier 2), some are a lot tougher (Tier 3). All champions have a set of buffs — basic abilities and/or resistances — and many (11/20 varieties) have an extra vulnerability to a certain type of magical damage. Tier 2 and 3 champions gain extra abilities on top of these. The more dangerous champions are only encountered at higher difficulty settings.
For a normal mob or yellow-named champion, the color and size of crown designates whether it is Tier 1, Tier 2 or Tier 3:
Orange-named (mini-boss) champions always wear the red crown, but may be either Tier 1, Tier 2 or Tier 3, subject to the difficulty setting.
crown_definitions: A single-pointed yellow crown indicates it is Tier 1
A tri-pointed orange crown indicates it is Tier 2
A tri-pointed red crown with a central gem indicates it is Tier 3

Players can see the variety of Champion they are facing by looking at the creature's title, and additional detail can be found in the examination window. All champions receive the basic champion buff, Damage Boost - I deal extra damage.
Many have True Sight, making Invisibility ineffective against them:

paragraphs: Concealment in DDO refers to Concealment Miss Chance
It is one of the three major Miss chance checks in game, along with Incorporeal and Dodge, that can occur during an attack if the conditions for its occurance is met. Concealment comes in two forms:
bullets: A beneficial (buff) form that is applied to players and allies, through equipped items or effects, that forces enemy attacks on the beneficiary to include a check for Concealment Miss Chance.

An negative (debuff) form, that is an effect which is applied to enemies via a negative condition, forcing their attacks to include a check for Concealment on all those they attack whilst the negative condition persists.
exact_source_sections.following_paragraph: When the trigger for Concealment is activated, the attack must pass a roll that is greater than the total amount of Concealment that is protecting the target. Generally, multiple concealment bonuses of the same type do not stack, whether beneficial or offensive in nature, only the greatest concealment number applies. Currently almost all of them use the same bonus type - enhancement. (A couple of special exceptions are listed in the Stacking effects section below.)

paragraphs: Hate is the calculation of how much damage you've dealt to an NPC. In more recent updates, this is often referred to as Threat. The player having dealt the most damage to that NPC will be the target of his attacks and spells. At first, the NPC attacks are directed to the first one he saw, but as soon as he has been dealt damage by a player, the NPC may redirect his attack to the one at the top of his hate list. Each NPC has its own hate list of each known enemy, paired with the degree to which it hates that character. The list is constantly sorted by hate, and whoever is at the top of the list is chased and attacked. Any character who drops below 1 HP is removed from the list.
The ability to generate and retain hate of an enemy (whether you want the attention or not) is often known as "aggro".
There are three distinctly different channels of hate: Melee, Missile (aka "Ranged"), and Magic*.
(* Magic attacks that are made from a distance are still "Magic", not "Ranged")

If something that alters hate generation specifies one or two of those but not the third it should be assumed to specifically not affect all three. If something generically states that it "Increases/Decreases Hate generation", then it should be assumed to affect all three (unless there is a bug either with the text or the actual effect).

Monsters that can Teleport (e.g. Orthons), Burrow (e.g. Scorpions) or otherwise become briefly intangible (e.g. Ogre Magi) tend to reset aggro when they arrive.
